neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, year correct, date wrong by a week. MoCA 21/30 with losses in trail-making, cube, digit span backwards, serial sevens, fluency (10 animals) and delayed recall (2/5 unaided, 4/5 cued). No confabulation. Insight partial.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full with no nystagmus and no gaze palsy. Visual fields full. Face symmetric. Speech normal.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk with mild proximal wasting in the legs. Tone mildly increased in the legs. Strength 5/5 apart from 4+/5 hip flexion.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration reduced at the ankles and pinprick reduced to the mid-shin bilaterally, consistent with alcohol-related polyneuropathy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 3+ knees, absent ankle jerks, plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.coordination: Mild bilateral heel-to-shin ataxia with normal finger-to-nose; no intention tremor.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based and short-stepped with mild truncal instability; arm swing preserved. Tandem impossible. Romberg mildly positive.
neurological_exam.additional: No hepatomegaly, no spider naevi, no palmar erythema. No asterixis. Frontal release signs absent. Palpable pulses, regular at 80.

patient.chief_complaint: Three years of forgetfulness, slowness and unsteadiness, with a long history of heavy drinking
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Fabio Greco is a 66-year-old former lorry driver who attends with his brother. He drank between 100 and 120 grams of ethanol daily for about twenty-five years and has cut down to around forty grams in the past year. Over three years his brother has watched him become slower, more forgetful and less able to organise: he cannot manage his own benefits paperwork, forgets to pay for things, and has twice left the flat with the gas on. He is unsteady, particularly in the dark, and has fallen twice. He also reports numbness in his feet going back several years. His brother is clear that the cognitive decline has continued during the past year in which drinking has fallen substantially, which is the observation that brought them to the clinic: they expected improvement and did not see it. He had a withdrawal seizure six years ago and two withdrawal episodes. He denies double vision, has never had an episode of confusion with unsteadiness and eye movement problems, and has never been admitted for encephalopathy. His blood pressure has been recorded above 160 systolic on most visits and he takes amlodipine irregularly. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations and no dream enactment.

findings.type: White matter hyperintensity of presumed vascular origin
findings.location: Confluent periventricular and deep white matter

signal_characteristics.T2_FLAIR: Confluent hyperintensity with early deep confluence

findings.location: Left thalamus, right putamen, left corona radiata

signal_characteristics.Sagittal_T1: Atrophy of the superior vermis with widened folia — the pattern of alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration

signal_characteristics.SWI: Single deep focus of signal loss; no lobar microbleed, no cortical superficial siderosis

findings.location: Mild global with preserved medial temporal lobes; mamillary bodies normal

signal_characteristics.Coronal_T1: Hippocampi normal for age; mamillary bodies of normal volume, no periaqueductal signal change

additional_observations: Two processes are visible: a Fazekas 3 small-vessel burden with three lacunes and one deep microbleed, and superior vermian cerebellar atrophy typical of alcohol
Mamillary bodies are normal and there is no periaqueductal or medial thalamic signal change, so there is no imaging evidence of Wernicke-Korsakoff pathology
No cortical infarct; no restricted diffusion
mri.impression: Two coexisting processes: severe hypertensive small-vessel disease (Fazekas 3, three lacunes, one deep microbleed) accounting for the cognitive syndrome and the higher-level gait disorder, and alcohol-related superior vermian cerebellar atrophy accounting for the truncal component. No Wernicke-Korsakoff imaging features.

Reversible_cause_screen.clinical_significance: Low-normal on supplementation; no Wernicke syndrome clinically

labs.interpretation: MCV 99.4 fL with a GGT of 118 U/L and ALT 46 U/L reflects continuing alcohol intake. B12 214 pg/mL is low-normal and worth correcting. Thiamine is low-normal on supplementation with no clinical Wernicke syndrome. TSH, folate, RPR and HIV are normal or negative. LDL 128 mg/dL is above target. Nothing here identifies a reversible cause sufficient to explain the syndrome.

specialized_test.impression: A subcortical executive profile with preserved recognition memory and no confabulation. Korsakoff syndrome would present with a dense storage-type amnesia and confabulation, neither of which is present; the pattern matches the small-vessel burden.

findings.performance: Digit span backwards 0/1, serial sevens 2/3 — impaired
2/5 unaided, 4/5 cued — retrieval pattern, no confabulation

clinical_assessment.impression: MoCA 21/30 with an executive and retrieval profile, no confabulation and no amnestic-confabulatory syndrome. Alcohol-related cognitive impairment typically stabilises or improves with abstinence; continued progression across a year of substantially reduced intake, in a patient with untreated hypertension, points to an additional vascular process rather than to alcohol alone.

results.title: Diagnostic criteria for vascular cognitive disorders: a VASCOG statement
results.authors: Sachdev P, Kalaria R, O'Brien J, et al.
results.summary: Requires a cognitive syndrome documented on a validated instrument plus imaging or temporal evidence that cerebrovascular disease accounts for it.

results.title: Neuroimaging standards for research into small vessel disease (STRIVE-2)
results.authors: Duering M, Biessels GJ, Brodtmann A, et al.
results.summary: Defines and standardises the reporting of white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, perivascular spaces and cortical superficial siderosis.

vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

medication_review.proposed: review of the current medication list for anticholinergic burden
warnings: Anticholinergic load is a reversible contributor to cognitive impairment in this population and should be quantified before any new prescription.
medication_review.summary: No prohibitive interaction identified within the current list.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Vascular dementia — subcortical ischaemic (small-vessel) type from untreated hypertension, with a coexisting alcohol-related cerebellar syndrome and sensory polyneuropathy contributing to the gait disorder

differential.key_features: Twenty-five years of heavy intake makes this a genuine contender and it may contribute, but the deficit progressed across a year of substantially reduced intake, there is no Korsakoff phenotype, and the Fazekas 3 burden with three lacunes is sufficient on its own
No ophthalmoparesis, no acute confusional episodes in the history, no confabulation, normal mamillary bodies and no periaqueductal signal change; thiamine is low-normal on supplementation
Cue-responsive recall, preserved hippocampi and an executive-predominant profile
No stigmata of chronic liver disease, no asterixis, normal ammonia not required given the absence of any clinical or biochemical evidence of decompensation
B12 214 pg/mL is low-normal and warrants correction, but cannot account for a Fazekas 3 burden with three lacunes

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a collateral history from an informant who sees the patient daily: the shape of the decline (abrupt, stepwise or gradual), whether any step can be dated to a cerebrovascular event, and which instrumental activities have been lost
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Three years of progressive executive and psychomotor decline that has continued despite a year of substantially reduced drinking, with untreated hypertension throughout and a superimposed sensory neuropathy

optimal_actions.action: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MoCA 21/30 with an executive and retrieval profile and no confabulation; the deficit has progressed despite reduced alcohol intake

optimal_actions.action: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Macrocytosis and raised GGT confirm continuing alcohol intake; thiamine and B12 low-normal and correctable; no reversible cause sufficient to explain the syndrome, and LDL 128 mg/dL above target

optimal_actions.action: Perform timed gait and balance testing: the short-stepped, wide-based gait with preserved arm swing is part of the subcortical syndrome and separates it from the gait of normal pressure hydrocephalus and of parkinsonian disorders
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Timed-up-and-go 16.8 s with a mixed gait disorder — vascular, cerebellar and neuropathic components each identifiable

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms — FLAIR for white matter hyperintensity with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI to establish that the lesions are chronic, and SWI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis — together with the medial temporal atrophy grade
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Fazekas 3 small-vessel burden with three lacunes and a deep microbleed, plus alcohol-related superior vermian cerebellar atrophy, with normal mamillary bodies excluding Wernicke-Korsakoff pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Executive and processing-speed impairment with preserved recognition and no confabulation — a subcortical vascular profile rather than an amnestic-confabulatory one

optimal_actions.action: Confirm the diagnostic criteria applied and the current secondary-prevention targets against the guidelines
optimal_actions.expected_finding: VASCOG 2014 criteria and the 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention targets confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Review the medication list for anticholinergic burden and for the interaction between antithrombotic choice and the microbleed burden before prescribing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anticholinergic contributors identified and the antithrombotic choice reconciled with the imaging burden

optimal_actions.action: Treat both processes: intensify antihypertensive therapy with adherence support toward a systolic below 130 mmHg, start a high-intensity statin to reach an LDL below 70 mg/dL, refer for alcohol cessation with continued thiamine and B12 replacement, arrange smoking cessation, and provide falls prevention addressing all three gait components
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Both the vascular and the alcohol-related processes addressed, with blood pressure identified as the driver of the component that is still progressing

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis and its mechanism to the patient and the informant, and address driving, medication management, finances, advance care planning and caregiver support
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and informant engaged in care planning; safety domains addressed

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

sequence_constraints.reason: Document the cognitive deficit before attributing it: imaging read without a cognitive profile invites over-attribution of incidental white matter change

critical_actions: Establish whether the decline continued during the period of reduced alcohol intake, because that is what separates the two attributions
Look for the Korsakoff phenotype explicitly — confabulation, storage-type amnesia, mamillary body atrophy — rather than assuming alcohol explains any cognitive deficit in a drinker
Document the cognitive profile formally and exclude reversible causes including thiamine and B12
Obtain brain MRI and read it for two processes rather than one
Separate the components of the gait disorder, since each has its own management
Treat the untreated hypertension, which is driving the component that is still progressing
Refer for alcohol cessation and provide the vitamin replacement that prevents Wernicke syndrome
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute the whole syndrome to alcohol in a patient whose decline progressed while intake fell and whose blood pressure was never controlled
Do not give glucose-containing fluids before thiamine in a patient with chronic alcohol use
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines outside a managed withdrawal in a patient with this falls risk
Do not treat an unconfirmed Korsakoff syndrome as established in the absence of confabulation and with normal mamillary bodies
Do not omit the vascular risk-factor treatment because the alcohol history is prominent
key_reasoning_points: The temporal test is decisive: alcohol-related cognitive impairment stabilises or improves with reduced intake, so progression across a year of substantial reduction implicates a second, still-active process
Korsakoff syndrome has a positive phenotype — dense storage amnesia with confabulation and mamillary body atrophy — and its absence is informative rather than merely unproven
Two comorbid processes can each be identified on one MRI: a Fazekas 3 small-vessel burden and superior vermian cerebellar atrophy have different causes and different implications
Untreated hypertension in a patient whose drinking has fallen is the actionable driver, and adherence is the intervention
Attributing everything to alcohol is the failure mode this case is built around: it removes the treatable vascular diagnosis from view

red_herrings.data_point: Twenty-five years of heavy alcohol intake
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attributes the entire syndrome to alcohol and closes the assessment without treating the hypertension
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The decline continued through a year of substantially reduced intake, there is no Korsakoff phenotype, and the Fazekas 3 burden with three lacunes is independently sufficient — alcohol contributes to the cerebellar and neuropathic findings

red_herrings.intended_effect: Reinforces the alcohol attribution and is read as evidence about the cause of the dementia
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: These markers confirm continuing intake, which is worth addressing, but they say nothing about which process is producing the cognitive decline

key_educational_points: Progression during a period of reduced drinking is the argument that separates vascular from alcohol-related cognitive decline
Korsakoff syndrome should be diagnosed on its positive features, not assumed from a drinking history
One MRI can show two processes; superior vermian atrophy and small-vessel burden have different causes
A prominent alcohol history is the commonest reason a treatable vascular diagnosis is missed
